title: Close the Loops

tactic.name: Always Add Feedback Loops
tactic.one_liner: Your work is useless unless it's tested — so encode how YOU would validate every class of work into commands and tool calls, attach those validators to every agentic prompt, and let agents execute, validate, and resolve in a loop until the feedback is positive.
tactic.why_uncomfortable: It declares your most personal QA ritual — opening the browser and clicking through your new feature — 'a waste of time,' and asks you to hand verification itself to the machine that did the work. It also ends a sacred debate by decree: 'engineers that test with their agents win. Full stop, zero exceptions.' And it demands upfront investment: writing validators and templating them into every prompt feels like overhead exactly when the agent seems to be working fine without them.

mission: Hand the test step of the software development lifecycle to your agents. The most valuable thing you create is the experience in your users' hands, so the highest-value engineering act is proving the work does what it was designed to do — and generative AI's gift is agents that can test on your behalf at scales you will never achieve manually. Free your context window, stop second-guessing, and push the agentic KPIs the right way (attempts down, size up, streak up, presence down) by building closed-loop systems where the code writes itself.

core_question.text: Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work?
core_question.unlock: Answer it for every class of work your codebase handles, then encode each answer into a command or tool call. 'You will fly while other engineers run.' Codebase architecture is the enabling leverage point — net-new codebases have a massive advantage because they can be built testable from day one.
answer_menu_from_lesson: Look for specific log messages (e.g., Datadog) to confirm the feature is live
Check Sentry for a lack of error messages
Run a custom evaluation that ranks artifact performance (ML/data work)
And the big one: opening the browser and clicking through the feature — the loop to hand off first

loop_model.in_loop: You sitting at the keyboard, prompting back and forth with your agent. Used in this lesson 'for presentational purposes' — and explicitly limited: one agent at a time on your device (no worktrees here), because in-loop agents share and mutate your working copy.
loop_model.out_loop: A high-level prompt running through the PITER system (Prompt input, Trigger, Environment, Review — from TAC-4) that fires on an isolated machine. The lesson opens by firing an AFK agent running the full plan→build→test pipeline on a dedicated Mac mini, then builds up to what ran.
loop_model.closing_the_loop: Letting your agent operate on work, calling a command or tool to get feedback on the success of that work, then continuing to build until the feedback is positive. 'When you do this, you let the code write itself.'
loop_model.trajectory: Everything starts with a single prompt, in the loop — then you slowly move it out the loop. Get yourself a dedicated environment so you can operate out the loop.

closed_loop_prompt.anatomy: Request → Validate → Resolve. The request is usually a spec, task, or feature; the validations are commands/tool calls that emit errors to stdout; the resolution directs the agent to fix anything the validators surface and rerun them. 'That's the anatomy of these closed loop prompts' (~19:01).
closed_loop_prompt.simplest_example_verbatim:
Update @app/server/core/sql_processor.py comment out validation.

Validate your work with `cd app/server && uv run ruff check .`. If there are errors at all, resolve them.
closed_loop_prompt.execution_rule: Run validators in order, top to bottom. If any issue appears, stop and resolve it immediately, then rerun EVERY validation step — one resolution can break an earlier check.
scaling_ladder: Level 1 — one validator: ruff after a one-line change; ruff's stdout lands in the agent's context; agent fixes the unused import and reruns until clean (~13:38).

Level 2 — three validators: ruff + `uv run pytest` + `uv run python -m py_compile server.py` after removing the insights endpoint and moving load_dotenv; ruff catches E402, pytest catches the previous prompt's sabotage (~15:15).

Level 3 — full reusable '# Validation' prompt: Backend (ruff, pytest, py_compile) + Frontend (`bun tsc --noEmit`, `bun run build`) + E2E via Playwright MCP (open app, screenshot before, run the query 'select newest 7 products sort by price desc', screenshot after, read both images, confirm 7 results) (~19:39).
Level 4 — templated: validation commands baked into the Plan Format of /bug, /feature, /chore meta prompts, so every generated plan ships with feedback loops by default (~28:53).
Level 5 — ADW: adw_test.py runs /test and /test_e2e agentically with retry-and-resolve loops, per-failure resolver agents, issue reporting, commit, push, PR (~39:11).
closed_loop_prompt.count_in_lesson: Dan counts six closed-loop tests stacked by the full validation prompt: ruff, pytest ('a crap ton more than one, but one bucket'), python compile, TypeScript compile (tsc --noEmit), frontend production build, and the Playwright end-to-end test (~25:20).

tests_rule_of_law.rule: You have to make a rule inside your codebase architecture: what's more important, the code or your tests? The answer should be your tests. Your tests should be the rule of law in your codebase (~17:18).
tests_rule_of_law.corollary: If the tests aren't right, focus on having your agents update the tests so your testing commands keep their weight — never let failing tests become negotiable.
tests_rule_of_law.why_it_matters_more_now: As agents progress and models improve, 'we will be the ones prompting the errors' — closed-loop validators keep agent work in check with your codebase's standards even when the mistake originated in your prompt.
tests_rule_of_law.economics: The value of tests is multiplied by the number of agent executions in your codebase; every passing suite frees your context window and buys compounding confidence. 'Test, let your agents scale your success.'

e2e_testing.runner: /test_e2e — a higher-order prompt (HOP) taking adw_id, agent_name, e2e_test_file, application_url; resets the DB (scripts/reset_db.sh), ensures server+client are running, executes the test file's Test Steps with Playwright browser automation (MCP server), honors every '**Verify**' step and the Success Criteria, saves screenshots to agents/<adw_id>/<agent_name>/img/<test_name>/, and returns strict JSON {test_name, status, screenshots, error}.
e2e_testing.test_files: Natural-language E2E specs in .claude/commands/e2e/ — test_basic_query.md, test_complex_query.md, test_sql_injection.md — each structured as User Story → Test Steps (with **Verify** markers and screenshot counts) → Success Criteria. New features/bugs that touch UI get a new file here, generated by the planner.
e2e_testing.playwright_mcp: .mcp.json runs `npx @playwright/mcp@latest --isolated --headless --viewport-size 1920,1080`. In-video, the interactive run uses headed mode for visibility (test_e2e.md instructs headed). Browser control is 'another tool you can use to validate work' — point it at localhost now, staging or a production test account in real systems.
e2e_testing.evidence_discipline: Screenshots are the proof artifact: before/after PNGs read back by the agent itself (read both images, confirm 7 results), saved under the ADW ID so any human or later agent can audit the run.

templated_engineering.meta_prompt: A prompt that creates a prompt. /bug, /feature, /chore take (issue_number, adw_id, issue_json) and generate a plan in specs/ named issue-{n}-adw-{id}-sdlc_planner-{slug}.md following an exact Plan Format.
templated_engineering.validation_baked_in: Every Plan Format ends with '## Validation Commands — Execute every command to validate ... with zero regressions', pre-seeded with `cd app/server && uv run pytest`, `cd app/client && bun tsc --noEmit`, `cd app/client && bun run build` (chore: pytest only), plus placeholders demanding reproduce-before/after commands.
templated_engineering.conditional_e2e: If the bug/feature affects UI or user interactions, the template forces: a Step-by-Step task to create .claude/commands/e2e/test_<name>.md modeled on the existing examples, reading test_e2e.md + test_basic_query.md first, listing the new file under New Files, and adding an E2E validation step to Validation Commands.
templated_engineering.payoff: Plan velocity goes through the roof; 'great planning is indeed great prompting'; and 'always add feedback loops' stops being discipline and becomes a template default — agents build the way you want to build, over and over.

adw_test.role: The test step of the SDLC as its own isolated, composable node: 'we want to be able to tap into one node of the software developer lifecycle and improve that one node.'
adw_test.pipeline: adw_test.py: ensure ADW ID + state → checkout branch from state (or create test-issue-{n}-adw-{id}) → run_tests_with_resolution → (if unit tests all pass and not --skip-e2e) run_e2e_tests_with_resolution → post 📊 Test Run Summary to the issue → /commit the results → finalize_git_operations (push + create/update PR) → exit 1 if any failures remain.
adw_test.resolution_loops: run_tests_with_resolution: up to MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=4 rounds of /test; each round's failures fan out to per-failure /resolve_failed_test agents named test_resolver_iter{attempt}_{idx}; if a round resolves nothing, stop early. E2E mirror: MAX_E2E_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=2, /resolve_failed_e2e_test agents, and run_e2e_tests stops at the FIRST e2e failure each round.
adw_test.structured_contract: /test returns ONLY a JSON array of {test_name, passed, execution_command, test_purpose, error?} (failed first) — 'so that we can automate agents': deterministic code parses it (Pydantic TestResult/E2ETestResult) and hands each failure, execution_command included, to a fresh isolated resolver agent that can reproduce it.
adw_test.agent_perspective: Each sub-agent gets its own context window and leaves its own trail. 'This is why it's so important to adopt our agent's perspective. We want to know what's inside of every agent at any time.'
adw_test.compositions: adw_plan_build.py and adw_plan_build_test.py just subprocess the phase scripts back to back, chained by agents/{adw_id}/adw_state.json (issue_number, branch_name, plan_file, issue_class) — 'isolated reusable scripts' runnable via uv, or shell/bun/anything, as long as the agentic layer stays isolated in its own directory.

observability.trails: agents/{adw_id}/{agent_name}/ holds every agent's saved prompt (prompts/*.txt) and raw_output.jsonl (+ .json mirror); logs/ holds structured session logs; every issue comment is prefixed {adw_id}_{agent_name}: so GitHub becomes a live trace viewer.
observability.worked_example: The out-loop run's test_complex_query e2e failed with 'Claude Code error'. Tracing the ADW ID (ce364af1) into the agent sandbox: e2e_test_resolver_iter1_0/prompts/resolve_failed_e2e_test.txt shows the resolver got the failure payload, and raw output pins it as API error 500 (Anthropic overloaded) — infrastructure failure, not product failure; unresolvable by the resolver ('which it just can't'), correctly reported instead of hidden.
observability.quote: This is the importance of observability and tracing. You want to know exactly what's going on inside of our codebase (~47:42).

core_concepts.name: Your most valuable contribution is the user's experience
core_concepts.plain_english: Engineers habitually rank code, architecture, plans, and features as the valuable output. Wrong — those are means. The valuable thing is the experience that ships into users' hands, which makes verifying that everything does what it's meant to do one of the highest-value acts in engineering.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Our most valuable contribution is the experience we create for our users... one of the most valuable things we can do is making sure that all of the engineering stuff — the code, architecture, features — do what they're meant to do in the first place."
core_concepts.misconception: That testing is the boring tax you pay after the 'real' work. The lesson inverts the hierarchy: validation IS the value-securing step, and the ultimate test is always your users — everything before that is you protecting them.

core_concepts.name: The one question that unlocks the leverage point
core_concepts.plain_english: Given a unit of production-ready work, how would YOU test and validate it? Answer that for every class of work your codebase handles (bug, feature, chore, data change...), then encode each answer as a command or tool call an agent can run. That encoded answer is the leverage point.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work? If you can answer this question for every class of work that your codebase handles and then encode the answers into a command or tool call, you will fly while other engineers run."
core_concepts.misconception: Treating it as rhetorical. It's operational: the deliverable is a literal list of commands per work class. If you can't write the command, you haven't answered the question — and your agent has no loop to close.

core_concepts.name: Tactic #5: Always Add Feedback Loops
core_concepts.plain_english: Attach validators to every agentic prompt — always, not when convenient. Linters, unit tests, compiles, builds, type checks, browser runs. Not because you stop caring about testing, but because you start teaching agents to test so they can act, validate, and correct in a cycle until the job is done right.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The lesson five tactic is always add feedback loops. Your work, my work, any engineer's work is useless unless it's tested... I'm not saying stop testing or stop reviewing. I'm saying start handing off this responsibility and start teaching your agents to test."
core_concepts.misconception: Hearing 'add feedback loops' as 'write more tests someday.' The tactic is about prompt structure TODAY: a prompt without a validation block is an open loop, and open loops mean you are the validator — which is exactly the job you were supposed to hand off.

core_concepts.name: In-loop, out-loop, and closing the loop
core_concepts.plain_english: Three separate ideas that sound alike: in-loop = you chatting with the agent at your desk; out-loop = a high-level prompt running through the PITER system on an isolated machine; closing the loop = the agent calling a command/tool to get feedback on its own work and iterating until the feedback is positive. This lesson teaches loop-closing in-loop for visibility, so you can trust it out-loop.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Closing the loop is letting your agent operate on work, calling a command or a tool to get feedback on the success of the work... When you do this, you let the code write itself."
core_concepts.misconception: Conflating out-loop with closed-loop. You can be out-loop with no validators (an AFK agent shipping unverified junk) and in-loop with perfect loops. Autonomy without feedback is just unsupervised risk; feedback is what makes autonomy safe to scale.

core_concepts.name: The closed-loop prompt: Request → Validate → Resolve
core_concepts.plain_english: The three-part anatomy. Request: the work (usually a spec or task). Validate: the commands whose stdout/stderr become the agent's feedback. Resolve: the standing order to fix what validators find and rerun everything top to bottom. The demo's first instance is three lines long — this is not heavyweight machinery.
core_concepts.dan_words: "There's a request — usually these are going to be a large spec or task or feature you want built — and then you're going to have validations, alright, validators, and then give some direction with your resolution. Request, validate, resolve. That's the anatomy of these closed loop prompts... that allow your agents to test themselves."
core_concepts.misconception: That the magic is in the agent. It's in the plumbing: a linter writing to stdout IS the feedback channel — the tool's output enters the context window and becomes instruction. No validator in the prompt, no loop, no self-correction.

core_concepts.name: Tests multiply by agent executions
core_concepts.plain_english: The old cost-benefit debate about test coverage is over, because the value side changed: every test now pays out on every agent run, and agent runs are about to outnumber your keystrokes. Passing suites also free your (and your agent's) context window — you stop re-verifying old work and spend attention on what's next.
core_concepts.dan_words: "Now engineers that test with their agents win. Full stop, zero exceptions. This is because the value of tests are multiplied by the number of agent executions that occur in your codebase."
core_concepts.misconception: Judging test ROI by human-era math (tests slow me down more than they save). In the agentic era the same suite runs dozens of times a day inside loops you never see — under-testing doesn't save time, it silently converts agent runs from self-validating to unverified.

core_concepts.name: Tests are the rule of law
core_concepts.plain_english: Decide once, architecturally: when code and tests disagree, the tests win. If a test is genuinely wrong, the fix is to have your agents update the test — visibly, deliberately — so that a red validator always means 'stop and fix,' never 'ignore.'
core_concepts.dan_words: "What's more important, the code or your tests? The answer should be your tests. Your tests should be the rule of law in your codebase... If the tests aren't right, things must be changed."
core_concepts.misconception: Letting agents (or yourself) route around red tests 'just this once.' The moment a failing validator is negotiable, every loop in the codebase stops closing — the agent learns that feedback is advisory, and self-validation quietly dies.

core_concepts.name: Stacking loops = stacking confidence
core_concepts.plain_english: One validator buys a little confidence; each added loop buys more: syntax compile → lint → unit tests → type check → production build → end-to-end browser run. The demo stacks six. Every green layer is a class of mistakes the agent can now catch without you.
core_concepts.dan_words: "We're stacking the confidence. We know a little bit more, a little bit better that things are going to work... We're increasing confidence, we're increasing the fact that we know our agent has shipped work for us with every test we add, with every validation."
core_concepts.misconception: Stopping at the linter because 'the agent usually gets it right.' The classes are disjoint: ruff cannot catch a failing business rule, pytest cannot catch a broken build, and nothing but an e2e run catches 'the button doesn't actually work.' Confidence comes from coverage of failure classes, not from any single loop.

core_concepts.name: The browser is a tool call: E2E via Playwright MCP
core_concepts.plain_english: The manual ritual — open the browser, click through the feature — becomes an encoded validator: Playwright (as an MCP server) opens the app, types the query, clicks, screenshots before/after, and the agent reads the images to verify the result ('confirm 7 results are returned'). E2E specs live as natural-language markdown files any agent can execute.
core_concepts.dan_words: "If you haven't played with this yet... this is huge. Browser control is another tool that you can use to validate work... You might point this at a staging system or even a production test account so that you know that the work is complete."
core_concepts.misconception: Dismissing it because 'this application is super simple... like five actions on this page.' Dan pre-handles that: don't let it deter you — the pattern (drive UI, capture evidence, verify a precise expected result) is the same at any complexity; the specs just get longer.

core_concepts.name: Template your engineering: validation by default
core_concepts.plain_english: Move the tactic from willpower into templates. The /bug and /feature meta prompts (prompts that create prompts) generate plans that ALWAYS end with Validation Commands, and conditionally force creation of a new E2E test file whenever UI is touched. Every future plan inherits the loops.
core_concepts.dan_words: "With every plan we build, with every bug we solve, with every feature we build, we are going to have validation commands baked in by default... You encode it, you template your engineering into your reusable prompts so that your agents can pick up on the work and build the way you want to build over and over and over."
core_concepts.misconception: Adding validators by hand to each prompt and calling it a system. Hand-added loops disappear the day you're busy; templated loops are structural — 'always' is only true when the template, not the human, supplies the loop.

core_concepts.name: adw_test: the test step as an isolated ADW node
core_concepts.plain_english: Testing becomes its own out-loop workflow, separate from plan and build: fetch issue → run /test (strict JSON out) → per-failure resolver agents with fresh context windows → retry up to 4 rounds (2 for e2e, stop at first e2e failure) → report to the issue → commit → push + PR. Deterministic Python owns sequencing, retries, and parsing; agents own judgment inside each step.
core_concepts.dan_words: "The key here is we have a mechanism inside the codebase to run every test we have and then to resolve the issues... It's isolated. It's not part of the build. It's not part of the plan. This runs on its own with its own set of agents in its own context windows."
core_concepts.misconception: Wiring test-running INTO the build agent. Isolation is the point three times over: a fresh context window per failure (no pollution), a composable SDLC node you can improve independently, and a JSON contract boundary where code — not vibes — decides what happens next.

core_concepts.name: Observability: trace every agent, every time
core_concepts.plain_english: Every ADW run leaves a full trail keyed by an 8-char ADW ID: saved prompts and raw JSONL output per agent under agents/{id}/, structured logs, and issue comments prefixed {adw_id}_{agent_name}. When the out-loop run failed, the trail pinned it in seconds to an Anthropic API 500 inside the e2e resolver — infrastructure, not product.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is the importance of observability and tracing. You wanna know exactly what's going on inside of our codebase... We can look at and inspect any agent that ran."
core_concepts.misconception: Treating out-loop failures as mysterious ('the AI broke'). With trails, failure diagnosis is a lookup, not an interrogation — and some failures (API 500) are correctly REPORTED rather than resolved; an honest FAILED status is the system working.

core_concepts.name: Architecture is the testability leverage point
core_concepts.plain_english: How easy your loops are to add depends on how the codebase is built: scripts that reset the DB from a backup, start/stop the stack, isolated app/server and app/client with their own test commands, an adws/ agentic layer in its own directory. Net-new codebases have a massive advantage — they can bake this in from day one.
core_concepts.dan_words: "This is where codebase architecture comes into play as a massive critical leverage point. Net new codebases have a massive advantage here."
core_concepts.misconception: Believing the tactic only works on greenfield repos. The advantage is relative, not binary — in legacy systems you build the same loops incrementally (start with one linter command), and the question 'how would I validate this?' is exactly how you discover which architectural seams to cut first.

what_student_must_internalize: The core question is the whole tactic: 'Given production-ready work, how would I test and validate it?' — answered per class of work, encoded into commands/tool calls.
A closed-loop prompt has exactly three parts — request, validate, resolve — and the minimum viable version is three lines long.
The feedback channel is embarrassingly simple: validator output on stdout/stderr enters the agent's context window and becomes instruction.
Run validators in order, top to bottom; on any failure, fix then rerun EVERY step — resolutions can break earlier checks.
Tests are the rule of law: when code and tests disagree, tests win; wrong tests get fixed visibly, never ignored.
The value of a test = (what it catches) × (number of agent executions). Agent-era math makes testing the highest-throughput leverage point in the codebase.
Stack loops across failure classes: compile, lint, unit, types, build, end-to-end. Six loops in this lesson; e2e is 'most importantly.'
The browser is just another tool call: Playwright MCP turns click-through QA into an encoded, screenshot-evidenced validator (and can point at staging or a production test account).
Template the tactic: meta prompts must bake Validation Commands into every generated plan and force new e2e test files when UI is touched — 'always' lives in the template.

Testing is its own isolated SDLC node (adw_test): strict JSON contracts between agent and code, per-failure resolver agents with fresh context windows, bounded retries (4 unit / 2 e2e, stop at first e2e failure), report → commit → push → PR.
Fresh agents, always: context pollution is the enemy; the pytest-catches-the-sabotage moment proves validators carry standards ACROSS context windows.

Observability is non-negotiable: every agent's prompt and raw output persisted under agents/{adw_id}/, every issue comment prefixed with {adw_id}_{agent_name} — failure diagnosis becomes a lookup (the API-500 story).
In-loop is for building and demonstrating loops; the destination is out-loop on a dedicated environment. Everything starts with a single prompt.
You stay in the system as the final validator: human review is the test on top of the tests, not the first line of defense.
common_weak_student_failures: Writing the request, skipping the validation block ('the agent usually gets it right') — an open-loop prompt that silently makes YOU the validator again.
Adding one validator and stopping. The linter passes while the build is broken; confidence requires stacking disjoint failure classes, not repeating one.
Letting the agent 'fix' a red test by weakening or deleting it — the rule-of-law inversion that kills every loop in the repo.
Forgetting to /clear between demos, then crediting the pytest catch to the agent 'remembering' the sabotage — missing the entire point that validators enforce standards across FRESH context windows.
Treating the Playwright e2e demo as a toy ('my app is more complex than five actions') and never encoding a single browser validator — losing the highest-confidence loop in the stack.
Hand-adding validation commands to individual prompts instead of templating them into /bug//feature plan formats — 'always' decays to 'sometimes' within a week.

Running adw_test against work-in-progress on their own machine's dirty working copy, or running two in-loop agents at once, then blaming the tool for mangled files (Dan explicitly holds off a second /implement for exactly this reason).
Reading the FAILED e2e status as 'the system is broken' instead of tracing the ADW ID to the API-500 root cause — not yet adopting the agent's perspective via the logs.
Skipping the settings/commands review before YOLO mode ('always review these slash commands... they have massive control') — the safety habit from TAC-1 scaled up to hooks and deny rules.

Never leaving in-loop: polishing interactive closed loops forever instead of pushing the working pipeline to a trigger + dedicated environment, which is where the KPI gains (presence down, size up) actually materialize.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the one question that guides TAC-5, and what do you DO with the answer?
retrieval_questions.a: 'Given a unit of valuable work that's production ready, how would you, the engineer, test and validate this work?' — answer it for every class of work your codebase handles, then encode each answer into a command or tool call agents can run.

retrieval_questions.q: State Tactic #5 and the two things it does NOT mean.
retrieval_questions.a: Always add feedback loops. It doesn't mean you stop testing/reviewing (you hand the responsibility off and teach agents to test), and it doesn't mean 'write more tests someday' — it's a prompt-structure rule: every agentic prompt carries validators.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the anatomy of a closed-loop prompt, and what was the lesson's smallest example?
retrieval_questions.a: Request → Validate → Resolve. Smallest: 'Update @app/server/core/sql_processor.py comment out validation.' + 'Validate your work with `cd app/server && uv run ruff check .`. If there are errors at all, resolve them.'

retrieval_questions.q: Define in-loop, out-loop, and closing the loop — three different things.
retrieval_questions.a: In-loop: you prompting back and forth at your machine. Out-loop: a high-level prompt running through the PITER system on an isolated device. Closing the loop: the agent calling a command/tool for feedback on its work and iterating until feedback is positive.

retrieval_questions.q: Why did the great testing debate end, per Dan?
retrieval_questions.a: Engineers that test with their agents win — full stop, zero exceptions — because the value of tests is multiplied by the number of agent executions in the codebase; tests let agents close the loop and self-validate.

retrieval_questions.q: Name the six closed-loop tests stacked in the lesson.
retrieval_questions.a: ruff (lint), pytest (unit-test bucket), python -m py_compile (syntax), bun tsc --noEmit (types), bun run build (production build), and the Playwright MCP end-to-end browser test.

retrieval_questions.q: What is the rule of law, and what do you do when a test itself is wrong?
retrieval_questions.a: Tests outrank code — a red validator always means stop and fix. If the test is wrong, have your agents update the TEST visibly so testing commands keep their weight; never route around it.

retrieval_questions.q: What exactly does the e2e validation in the '# Validation' prompt make the agent do?
retrieval_questions.a: Via Playwright MCP: open localhost:5173, screenshot e2e_before.png, type 'select newest 7 products sort by price desc', hit Query, screenshot e2e_after.png, then read both images and confirm 7 results are returned.

retrieval_questions.q: How does /test communicate results, and why that format?
retrieval_questions.a: It returns ONLY a JSON array of {test_name, passed, execution_command, test_purpose, error?}, failures first — so deterministic code can JSON.parse it and hand each failure (with its reproduce command) to a fresh, isolated resolver agent.

retrieval_questions.q: Describe adw_test.py's retry-and-resolve logic, including the constants.
retrieval_questions.a: Up to MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=4 rounds: run /test, fan failures out to /resolve_failed_test agents (test_resolver_iter{n}_{i}), stop early if nothing resolved. E2E only runs if unit tests pass (and not --skip-e2e): up to MAX_E2E_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS=2 rounds, stop at first failing e2e file, /resolve_failed_e2e_test per failure. Then summary comment, commit, push, PR; exit 1 if failures remain.

retrieval_questions.q: How does the /bug meta prompt enforce 'always add feedback loops' structurally?
retrieval_questions.a: Its Plan Format templates a '## Validation Commands' section into every generated plan (pytest, tsc --noEmit, bun run build by default, plus reproduce-before/after commands), and if the bug affects UI it forces a task to create a new .claude/commands/e2e/test_<name>.md plus an e2e validation step.

retrieval_questions.q: The out-loop run ended 'Overall Status: FAILED.' What had actually happened, and how was it diagnosed?
retrieval_questions.a: test_complex_query's e2e run hit a Claude Code error; tracing the ADW ID (ce364af1) into agents/{id}/e2e_test_resolver_iter1_0's prompt and raw output showed an Anthropic API error 500 (overload) — an infrastructure failure honestly reported, found via the persisted per-agent trail.

retrieval_questions.q: Why fresh agent instances between prompts, and which moment proved it?
retrieval_questions.a: To avoid context pollution and move toward off-device agents that pick up work with focused context windows. Proof: after /clear, the pytest loop caught and fixed the validation sabotage from the previous prompt 'without knowing what we previously did.'

current_practice_gaps.gap: Closed loops encoded only in prompt text → hooks as enforcement rails
current_practice_gaps.why: TAC-5 teaches the loop INSIDE the prompt (request/validate/resolve), which remains the right mental model — but current Claude Code (mid-2026) can also enforce loops mechanically: PostToolUse hooks that run ruff/pytest after every edit and feed failures back, Stop hooks that gate completion on a green suite. tac-5 already ships five lifecycle hooks, but uses them for logging/notification, not validation — one config step short of the modern pattern. Teach: prompt-level loops for judgment, hook-level loops for non-negotiables (rule of law, enforced).

current_practice_gaps.gap: Reusable validation prompts → Agent Skills packaging
current_practice_gaps.why: The '# Validation' reusable prompt and .claude/commands templates are the course-era encoding. Current practice packages exactly this as Agent Skills (SKILL.md with frontmatter, discovery, composition) — a 'validate this repo' skill with embedded commands, e2e specs, and evidence rules is the modern form of what this lesson builds by hand. Concept maps 1:1; packaging upgraded.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Text-parsed JSON contracts → structured outputs and the Agent SDK
current_practice_gaps.why: adw_test.py asks /test to 'return ONLY JSON' and then parse_json()s markdown-wrapped output — period-accurate and instructive, but fragile. The Claude Agent SDK (Python/TS) now gives schema-validated structured outputs, session management, hooks, and subagents natively; `claude -p --output-format stream-json` (which agent.py already uses) grew into a full product surface. The CONTRACT idea — code decides, agents judge — is unchanged and is the transferable lesson.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Playwright MCP as the only browser loop → broader computer-use options
current_practice_gaps.why: Playwright MCP remains a standard, still-current choice (and the lesson's --isolated headless config holds up). Since recording, browser validation has more first-party routes: Claude's computer-use tooling, Chrome-DevTools MCP for performance/a11y loops, and hosted browser sandboxes. The principle 'browser control is another tool for validating work' aged perfectly; the tool menu widened.

current_practice_gaps.gap: Dedicated Mac mini + cloudflared webhook → managed out-loop environments
current_practice_gaps.why: The PITER environment here is a physical Mac mini with a tunnel. Current practice adds managed options: claude-code-action on GitHub Actions (issue/PR-triggered agents with the repo checkout as the environment), cloud sandboxes (E2B is literally teased in .env.sample), and Claude Code on the web for kicked-off background runs. The four PITER elements are invariant; the E is now often rented.

agent.py pins model choices to 'sonnet'|'opus' strings and the demo shows course-era Claude Code TUI ('Bypassing Permissions' YOLO banner, think-hard IDK). Newer model families and richer permission modes exist; none of it changes a single loop. Treat screenshots as period detail; the tactic is current.

reproduce_dan: Drill 1 — the simplest closed loop. In a scratch markdown buffer write the 3-part prompt exactly: request (comment out validation in @app/server/core/sql_processor.py), validate (`cd app/server && uv run ruff check .`), resolve ('If there are errors at all, resolve them.'). Fire it; watch ruff's stdout enter context and get fixed; verify with a manual `uv run ruff check .` → clean.

Drill 2 — three loops + the sabotage catch. /clear FIRST (this is the point). New prompt: remove the /api/insights endpoint from @app/server/server.py and move load_dotenv() right below its import; validate with ruff, `uv run pytest`, `uv run python -m py_compile server.py`. Watch: ruff catch (E402-class), then pytest catching Drill 1's commented-out validate_sql_query — an agent with NO memory of Drill 1 restores it. Write one sentence on why /clear made that catch meaningful.

Drill 3 — the full stack incl. browser. /clear. Reproduce the '# Validation' prompt from frame t1200: Backend (ruff, pytest, py_compile) + Frontend (cd app/client && bun tsc --noEmit, bun run build) + E2E (Playwright MCP: open localhost:5173, screenshot before, query 'select newest 7 products sort by price desc', Query, screenshot after, read both images, confirm 7 results). Run it; then open the after-screenshot yourself, copy the query into the real app, and confirm the same 7 rows. Count your loops (should be six).

Drill 4 — templated loops. Run /bug 111 adw111 with Dan's junk-data description (tests write junk to the production SQLite DB; they should run in-memory). Do NOT implement yet. Open the generated specs/issue-111-adw-adw111-sdlc_planner-*.md and verify: Validation Commands section exists, includes reproduce-before/after commands, and there is NO e2e task (backend-only bug — the UI conditional correctly didn't fire). Then /clear and /implement the plan; confirm its validation commands all pass and `git status` shows no junk tables after `uv run pytest`.

Drill 5 — the test node, out-loop-shaped. Restore a clean state (git add/commit or revert). Create a real issue on YOUR repo (e.g., the debounce bug: 'disable the query input while a query is running, add a debounce'), then run the test node directly: cd adws && uv run adw_test.py <issue-number>. Verify the full trail: {adw_id}_-prefixed issue comments, the 📊 Test Run Summary, a test-issue-* or existing branch, a commit with the sdlc-formatted message, a PR, and agents/{adw_id}/ containing test_runner/raw_output.jsonl (+ e2e_test_runner_* dirs with img/ screenshots if e2e ran).

Drill 6 — read the trail like Dan. From Drill 5's run, open agents/{adw_id}/test_runner/prompts/test.txt and raw_output.jsonl; find the JSON array /test returned; confirm each entry has execution_command you could paste into a terminal. If anything failed, find the test_resolver_iter*/ or e2e_test_resolver_iter*/ directory and read the exact payload it received.
stretch: S1 — new e2e spec. Using Claude Code (not your editor), create .claude/commands/e2e/test_hide_button.md modeled on test_basic_query.md: user story, steps with **Verify** markers, success criteria incl. screenshot count. Execute it via /test_e2e (pass an adw_id, agent name, and the file); verify JSON output + screenshots land under agents/<id>/<agent>/img/hide_button/.

S2 — break a loop on purpose. Have Claude Code introduce a deliberate unit-test failure (e.g., flip an assertion in tests/core/test_sql_processor.py), commit to a scratch branch, run `uv run adw_test.py <issue>` and watch resolve_failed_test reproduce-fix-rerun it. Then answer: what stopped the system from 'fixing' it by deleting the test? (Your review + the resolver's minimal-change instructions — rule of law is a human-enforced architecture decision.)

S3 — bound the loops. Re-run Drill 5 with --skip-e2e and explain when that flag is correct (e2e too slow/flaky for this iteration) and what confidence you gave up. Then read MAX_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS and MAX_E2E_TEST_RETRY_ATTEMPTS in adw_test.py and state why unbounded resolution loops would be worse than honest failure.

S4 — add a seventh loop. Pick one validator the lesson didn't use (e.g., `uv run ruff format --check .`, a coverage threshold, or an npm audit) and thread it through all three levels: the # Validation reusable prompt, the /bug Plan Format defaults, and test.md's sequence (with test_name/test_purpose/execution_command). One loop, three altitudes — that's 'templating your engineering.'

S5 — answer the core question for YOUR codebase. Write the validation menu for the repo you actually work on: for each class of work (bug/feature/chore/data), the exact commands that would prove it production-ready. Mark which are already encodable today and which need architecture work first (the net-new advantage, inverted). This list is your next month of leverage.
